content: The data presented outlines the adverse events and treatment outcomes associated with various regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB), particularly focusing on the BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) and its comparison to WHO-recommended long and short regimens. 1. Adverse Events (AEs): Peripheral neuropathy was reported in 16% of patients receiving the BPaL regimen, with higher rates (22%) in certain subgroups. This condition was less common in other regimens. Optic neuritis occurred in 1% of patients on BPaL, with slightly higher rates (2-5%) in specific subgroups. Myelosuppression was observed in 5% of patients on BPaL, with no significant occurrences in comparator regimens. Hepatotoxicity was reported in 12% of patients on BPaL, with similar rates in comparator regimens (11-13%). QT prolongation, a cardiac-related adverse event, was not observed in any of the regimens studied. 2. Treatment Discontinuation Due to AEs: Linezolid discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 14% of patients on BPaL, with higher rates (17-20%) in certain subgroups. Peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis were the most common reasons for discontinuation in the BPaL group. 3. Efficacy of BPaL Regimen: The BPaL regimen demonstrated higher treatment success rates compared to WHO-recommended long regimens (18-24 months) and short regimens (9-11 months). BPaL showed lower rates of treatment failure, recurrence, death, and loss to follow-up compared to the WHO long regimen. The success rate was consistent across most subgroups, except for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where no patients were included in the intervention group. 4. Comparison of Regimens: The BPaL regimen (600 mg linezolid for 26 weeks) was compared to WHO long and short regimens. The BPaL regimen showed better outcomes in terms of treatment success and lower adverse events requiring discontinuation. Variability in outcomes was noted between study sites, with South African sites reporting fewer cases of hepatotoxicity and higher rates of treatment step-down compared to other sites. 5. Limitations and Certainty of Evidence: Observational studies formed the basis of much of the data, leading to potential biases such as confounding and misclassification. Small sample sizes in the BPaL group (e.g., 33 patients in some analyses) resulted in imprecision and limited the ability to adjust for confounding factors. Variability in effect estimates across cohorts in the WHO dataset contributed to inconsistency in the findings. 6. WHO Guidelines and Recommendations: The WHO consolidated guidelines on DR-TB treatment (2022 update) recommend the use of all-oral regimens, including BPaL, for specific patient populations. The BPaL regimen is particularly recommended for patients with pulmonary pre-XDR-TB (MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance) and fluoroquinolone-susceptible disease. 7. Subgroup Analyses: In patients with fluoroquinolone-susceptible TB, the BPaL regimen showed superior outcomes compared to the WHO short regimen. The inclusion of fluoroquinolone-resistant TB in some analyses allowed for larger sample sizes and more robust comparisons. 8. Conclusion: The BPaL regimen offers a shorter, effective treatment option for DR-TB with higher success rates and manageable adverse events compared to traditional WHO regimens. Further research is needed to address limitations in the evidence, particularly regarding small sample sizes and variability across study sites. This detailed analysis highlights the potential of the BPaL regimen as a promising alternative for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis, with significant implications for global TB management strategies.
